processing: Usually eucommia leaf heated to stop browning, then rolled or cut and dried with methods borrowed from tea; a second high-temperature drying improves aroma and colour. The Korean form is noted as made from the bark.
harvest_season: Leaf is taken through the growing months; one published green-style method uses leaf from early June to mid October. No picking is widely prized.
appearance_dry: Cut dark olive-brown leaf pieces, sometimes with fine pale rubbery threads, as is typical of this plant.
appearance_liquor: Amber to reddish-brown, with well-refired lots redder and brighter.
taste_profile: Published work mainly notes a weak aroma in simple lots and some bitterness that makers try to reduce; expect a mild, roasted-herbal cup, as is usual for refired leaf tisanes.

brewing.notes: Boiling water and a long steep suit a mug or pot.

vintage_note: Not sold by vintage: it is bought as recent dried leaf, with a shelf-life date rather than a harvest year. Look at whether it is leaf or bark and whether it has been refired, since both change the cup.
description:
Du zhong cha is an infusion from Eucommia ulmoides, a Chinese tree better known for its bark in traditional medicine. Shaanxi lists it among its non-tea teas, and it is also developed and sold in Japan as tochu-cha and known in Korea as duchung-cha.

Most of it uses leaf treated much like tea, but simple tea-style processing leaves it with a weak aroma, poor looks and a dull liquor. So refined lots go through a high-temperature second drying, where time and heat strongly affect quality. Research on the kill-green step favours a gentle one to preserve active compounds.

Expect a mild, herbal cup with a toasted side from the refiring, and a bitterness that makers actively work to tame. Reports on its flavour are scarce, so treat that as a guide. It takes boiling water and a good long steep.

There is a modest result suggesting it can slightly lower blood pressure, and it is sold for many other things on limited research. Anyone on blood pressure medication should ask a doctor. Otherwise, choose it as a gentle caffeine-free drink.
history:
Eucommia is long established in Chinese medicine, but when the drink itself began is poorly recorded. Modern development is easier to trace: a Korean study from 1976 judged tea made from the leaf to be of acceptable quality.

Food science work in China from the early 2000s on looked at how to improve its processing, and the drink has since become a commercial product in China and Japan.
